passage:
On Pradeep's first day at the school in Andheri, he sat alone at the back. He wore a small hearing aid behind one ear, and when the class laughed at a joke, he looked around, lost.
Imran, ten, noticed. At lunch he sat opposite Pradeep, not beside him, so Pradeep could see his face. He spoke clearly, not shouting.
“Cricket after lunch. You want to bat?”
Pradeep hesitated. “I can't always hear the calls.”
“Then we'll use hands. Thumbs up for run, flat palm for stay.”
That afternoon Pradeep hit a four. Imran gave him the loudest thumbs up on the ground.

qa.q: Where did Imran sit at lunch?
qa.a: He sat opposite Pradeep, not beside him.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when the class laughed and he looked around?
qa.a: He felt lost and left out, not able to catch the joke.

qa.q: What did Imran do that made Pradeep feel included?
qa.a: He sat where Pradeep could see his face, spoke clearly and invented hand signals for the game.

qa.q: How might the other boys see Pradeep after the four?
qa.a: They probably see him as a good teammate, not as the new boy who sits alone.

grounding: A ten-year-old makes room for a new classmate who uses a hearing aid.

passage:
“Quiz teams! Groups of four,” said Ms Nair.
Everyone ran to their friends. Aditi, who had moved from Guwahati a month ago, stayed at her desk, looking at her pencil.
Yogesh, eleven, looked at his group. “We need one more.”
“Take Farhan,” said Rohit.
“Farhan's already with them.” Yogesh walked to Aditi's desk. “Want to be on our team?”
Aditi looked up. “I'm not very good at quizzes.”
“You know about Assam, right? There's always a geography round.”
She smiled a little. “I know about rhinos.”
“Perfect. Come on.”
In the geography round, Aditi answered two questions nobody else knew.

qa.q: How long ago had Aditi moved from Guwahati?
qa.a: A month ago.

qa.q: How was Aditi feeling when everyone ran to their friends?
qa.a: She felt shy and left out, staying at her desk looking at her pencil.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's invitation work?
qa.a: He asked her directly and pointed to something she knew, so she felt she had something to offer.

qa.q: How does Rohit see the team choice differently from Yogesh?
qa.a: Rohit only thinks of friends already picked, while Yogesh notices the new girl sitting alone and makes room for her.

grounding: An eleven-year-old invites a shy new classmate into a quiz team.

passage:
On our class trip to the Lodhi Garden, the plan was a treasure hunt across the lawns and up the steps of the old tomb. I was excited until I saw Tushar looking at the steps from his wheelchair.
I'm Chaitanya. I went to Ms Kapoor and asked if we could change the game. “What if the clues are only on the paths? And teams take turns reading the map?”
She said yes. Tushar read the map for our team. He was fast.
We didn't win. But at the end Tushar said it was the first trip where he didn't just watch. I felt proud of that, more than a prize.

qa.q: Where was the class trip?
qa.a: To the Lodhi Garden.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel at the end of the trip?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt proud that Tushar joined in rather than watched, more than about any prize.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do that helped include Tushar?
qa.a: Chaitanya asked the teacher to change the game so the clues were on the paths and teams took turns reading the map.

qa.q: How did the change affect Tushar?
qa.a: He felt included and useful, saying it was the first trip where he didn't just watch.

grounding: A student adapts a group game so a classmate who uses a wheelchair can take part.

passage:
I'm Disha, in Class 6 with Thomas. I've noticed he's different from some boys in our class.
When he joined the dance group, Varun called him “Thomasina.” Thomas just said, “I like dancing. You like cricket. Both are fine,” and kept practising.
When Gauri from our group was playing football and a boy said girls should go and skip, Thomas passed her the ball.
And when he needed my ruler, he asked first. He didn't just grab it, like others do.
I don't know what goes on in his head. But I trust him more than most.

qa.q: What did Varun call Thomas?
qa.a: He called him “Thomasina.”

qa.q: How did Thomas seem to feel about the teasing?
qa.a: He seemed calm and confident, not hurt enough to stop dancing.

qa.q: What could other boys learn from Thomas?
qa.a: That anyone can dance or play football, and that asking before taking shows respect.

qa.q: How does Disha see Thomas?
qa.a: Disha trusts and admires him more than most classmates.

grounding: A classmate observes an eleven-year-old boy showing courtesy and rejecting gender stereotypes.

passage:
Monday: In the school ground, Harish said, “Girls can't play kabaddi. It's rough.” Uma, ten, felt her face go hot. Gurleen pulled her arm. “Leave it.”
But Uma stepped forward. “We can. Can we try one game?”
Wednesday: The PE teacher set up a mixed game with clear rules: no pushing on the face, stop when someone says stop. Uma raided twice and got Harish out once. Harish laughed. “Okay, okay.”
Next Monday: Harish came up to Uma. “Can you show me that side step?”
Uma grinned. “Only if you show me your ankle hold.”

qa.q: What did Harish say about girls and kabaddi?
qa.a: He said girls can't play kabaddi because it's rough.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when Harish said girls can't play?
qa.a: She felt angry and embarrassed, her face going hot.

qa.q: What helped the boys and girls play respectfully together?
qa.a: A mixed game with clear rules and boundaries, such as stopping when someone says stop.

qa.q: How does Harish's view of Uma change?
qa.a: He moves from doubting girls to respecting Uma's skill and asking her to teach him.

grounding: Over a week a ten-year-old girl challenges a stereotype and builds respectful play with boys.

passage:
Nirmala, you asked if boys teased me when I was your age. Let your Simran Dadi tell you.
When I was twelve, in Jalandhar, a boy named Balwinder used to pull my plait every day in class and laugh. Everyone thought it was funny. I didn't.
One day I turned round and said, “Stop. I don't like it.” He looked shocked. Then he said sorry, and never did it again.
We became good friends, and years later he told me he had never thought about how it felt.
What I learnt, beti: you can say no, clearly and kindly, and a good person listens. Your Dadu listened too.

qa.q: What did Balwinder do every day?
qa.a: He pulled her plait every day in class and laughed.

qa.q: How did young Simran feel about Balwinder pulling her plait?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and upset, not finding it funny.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Simran clearly said “Stop. I don't like it,” which made Balwinder think and respect her boundary.

qa.q: How might Balwinder have felt when Simran told him to stop?
qa.a: He was shocked and then sorry, realising for the first time how it felt for her.

grounding: A grandmother tells how she set a boundary with a boy who teased her, and he respected it.

passage:
Last summer, when I was eleven, I was playing cricket alone in the lane and hit the ball into Chandrika-aunty's flower pot. It cracked in two.
Nobody saw. Aunty was at work. I could have just gone home.
I'm Deepak. I stood there for a long time. My stomach felt tight.
When she came home in the evening, I knocked. “Aunty, I broke your pot. I'm sorry.”
She looked at me, then at the pot. “You could have hidden it.”
“I know.”
She laughed and said I could help her repot the tulsi on Sunday. I did. It felt better than hiding.

qa.q: What did Deepak's ball crack?
qa.a: Chandrika-aunty's flower pot.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel standing in the lane after the pot broke?
qa.a: Deepak felt anxious and guilty, with a tight stomach.

qa.q: What choice did Deepak make, and why was it right?
qa.a: Deepak told Chandrika-aunty even though nobody had seen, which was honest and let them fix it together.

qa.q: How did Chandrika-aunty respond to Deepak's honesty?
qa.a: She was surprised, laughed and invited Deepak to help repot the tulsi.

grounding: An eleven-year-old admits breaking a neighbour's pot even though nobody saw.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 6. Ritu Sen.
During Tuesday's maths test, I was called out of the room for five minutes. I left the answer sheet on my desk by mistake.
When I came back, Shalini (eleven) came up to me after the test. She said she'd seen the sheet on my desk. She had turned it face down and had not looked. She was worried others might think she had.
I thanked her. I checked the room and decided to give a new test the next day to be fair.
Shalini's cheeks were pink, but she held her head up.
Next step: I'll keep my papers with me, and I've told Shalini's parents how honest she was.

qa.q: What had the teacher left on the desk?
qa.a: The answer sheet.

qa.q: How was Shalini feeling when she told the teacher?
qa.a: She felt nervous and worried that others might think she had looked.

qa.q: What made Shalini's choice honest?
qa.a: She turned the sheet face down without looking and told the teacher, even though nobody would have known.

qa.q: How might the other students feel about taking a new test?
qa.a: Some may be annoyed, but most may see it as fair.

grounding: A teacher records an eleven-year-old acting honestly when she could not be caught.

passage:
Saturday
I was cycling in the building parking and I scraped the side of a blue car with my pedal. A long white line.
There was nobody there. Not even the watchman.
I stood there for ages. My heart was thumping.
Then I went home and wrote a note: “Sorry, I scratched your car with my cycle. Please call my Mumma.” I wrote her number and taped it to the window.
In the evening Ishita-aunty from the fourth floor rang. Mumma went with me. Aunty said it was only a small scratch and thanked me for owning up.
I thought I'd feel terrible. I actually feel light. — Pema

qa.q: What colour was the car?
qa.a: It was a blue car.

qa.q: How did Pema feel before and after owning up?
qa.a: Pema felt nervous with a thumping heart before, and light and relieved after owning up.

qa.q: Why was writing the note the right choice?
qa.a: It was honest even though nobody saw, and it let the owner decide how to handle it.

qa.q: How did Ishita-aunty react to the note?
qa.a: She said it was a small scratch and thanked Pema for owning up.

grounding: A twelve-year-old admits scratching a car when nobody saw.

passage:
“A week without the phone? Just because I was ten minutes late?” Vaibhav, nine, slammed his bag down.
His brother Harsha, twelve, looked up from his homework. “What was the rule?”
“Home by six. I was ten past.”
“And the punishment for being late?”
“Mummy never said. She just decided.”
Harsha thought. “Ten minutes and a whole week does seem big. But you didn't call.”
Vaibhav went quiet. “My battery died.”
“Then tell her that. Ask if a day is fairer, and say you'll call next time.”
Vaibhav took a breath. “Will you come with me?”
“Okay. But you do the talking.”

qa.q: What time was Vaibhav supposed to be home?
qa.a: Home by six.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about losing the phone for a week?
qa.a: He felt angry and that it was unfair, slamming his bag.

qa.q: What did Harsha suggest to make it fairer?
qa.a: To explain the dead battery, ask if a day is fairer and promise to call next time.

qa.q: How might Mummy see Vaibhav's request?
qa.a: She may appreciate him explaining calmly and be willing to change the punishment.

grounding: Two brothers debate whether a punishment fits a small rule-break.

passage:
In Class 5, Kiran-ma'am had a rule: if anyone talked during silent reading, the whole class lost PE.
One Friday, one boy talked. We all lost PE. I'm Vaibhav, and I remember feeling it wasn't fair. I hadn't said a word.
At home, I thought about it. Punishing everyone made the others angry at that boy, not at the talking.
On Monday I asked Kiran-ma'am if I could say something. I said, “Maybe only the person who talks should lose PE, and the rest of us shouldn't.” My voice shook.
She thought, then asked the class to vote on a new rule. We did.

qa.q: What was the class rule about talking during silent reading?
qa.a: If anyone talked, the whole class lost PE.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel about losing PE?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt it was unfair and a bit angry, having not said a word.

qa.q: Why was Vaibhav's suggestion fairer?
qa.a: It only punished the person who broke the rule, not everyone.

qa.q: How did Kiran-ma'am respond to Vaibhav?
qa.a: She listened, thought and asked the class to vote on a new rule.

grounding: A student questions whether a group punishment is fair and suggests a better rule.

passage:
Student council note. Teacher adviser: Manoj Deshmukh.
This week the council discussed a case: a Class 6 boy broke a window while playing cricket at break. Some members wanted him suspended for a week.
Vikas (twelve) disagreed. He said suspension was too big for an accident, and wouldn't fix the window. He suggested the boy help the caretaker repair it and write an apology.
Others argued that rules need strong punishments. Vikas listened, then asked, “Does the punishment fit what happened?”
The council voted for Vikas's idea. The headmistress agreed.
Next step: I've asked Vikas to help draft a fairer list of consequences.

qa.q: What did some council members want for the boy?
qa.a: They wanted him suspended for a week.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel about the suspension idea?
qa.a: He felt uneasy that it was unfair and too big for an accident.

qa.q: What did Vikas suggest, and why was it fairer?
qa.a: Helping the caretaker repair the window and writing an apology, because it matched the accident and fixed the harm.

qa.q: How might the boy who broke the window feel about the council's decision?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and more willing to put things right.

grounding: A teacher notes a twelve-year-old arguing that a punishment should fit the mistake.

passage:
It was sports day, the sun was hot, and Lalremsiami, twelve, was about to run the relay when she felt something wet. She went pale. Her first period, and she had nothing with her.
Her friend Charu saw her face. “What's wrong?”
Lalremsiami whispered.
Charu didn't laugh. She took off her jacket and tied it round Lalremsiami's waist. “Come. Mrs Lalhmangaihi has pads in the sick room.”
The teacher gave her a pad and a clean pair of shorts, showed her the washroom and said, “This is normal. Nothing to be ashamed of. Next time, keep a spare in your bag.”
Lalremsiami ran the last leg of the relay after all.

qa.q: What did Charu tie around Lalremsiami's waist?
qa.a: She took off her jacket and tied it round Lalremsiami's waist.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when she realised her period had started?
qa.a: She felt shocked and embarrassed, going pale.

qa.q: What did Charu and the teacher do that helped?
qa.a: Charu stayed calm and helped discreetly, and the teacher gave supplies and said it was normal, with no shame.

qa.q: How might Charu feel helping her friend?
qa.a: Charu probably feels protective and glad she could help quietly, without any fuss.

grounding: Supported by a friend and teacher, a twelve-year-old handles her first period at school without shame.

passage:
At the school in Chennai, Ms Rehana, the counsellor, ran a Friday talk for Class 6 girls. A box on her desk was for questions without names.
Gopika, eleven, wrote hers during the break: Why do I smell sweaty now even when I'm not running? Is something wrong with me?
Ms Rehana read it out, without saying whose. “Good question. Nothing is wrong. As bodies grow, sweat changes. Bathing daily, clean clothes, and washing under the arms help. It happens to everyone, boys too.”
Some girls giggled, then nodded.
Gopika didn't feel embarrassed any more. She felt normal.

qa.q: What was the box on Ms Rehana's desk for?
qa.a: Questions without names.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after Ms Rehana answered her question?
qa.a: She felt relieved and normal instead of embarrassed.

qa.q: Why was the question box a good idea?
qa.a: It let students ask about body changes privately, without shame.

qa.q: How might the other girls feel after hearing the answer?
qa.a: They may feel relieved too, since many probably had the same question.

grounding: An eleven-year-old learns about body changes and hygiene without shame through an anonymous question box.

passage:
“Leela-didi, can I play football during my period? Sonam said you shouldn't run or it's dangerous.”
Leela put down her book. “That's not true, Mahima. Lots of girls play sports on their period.”
“Really?”
“If you feel okay, you can play. Some days you might feel tired or have cramps. Then you can rest.”
“What if it leaks?”
“Keep a spare pad and shorts in your bag. And tell your coach if you need a break. It's normal.”
Mahima thought. “And if it really hurts a lot?”
“Tell Mumma. If it keeps going or worries you, we'll check with the doctor.”
Mahima picked up her football boots. “Okay. Practice at four.”

qa.q: What did Sonam say about running during periods?
qa.a: Sonam said you shouldn't run or it's dangerous.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel about playing football during her period?
qa.a: She felt worried and unsure because of what Sonam said.

qa.q: What practical tips did Leela give?
qa.a: Keep a spare pad and shorts, rest if tired, tell the coach if needed, and tell Mumma if pain keeps going.

qa.q: How does Leela see Sonam's claim?
qa.a: Leela sees it as a myth and calmly corrects it.

grounding: An older sister corrects a period myth and helps an eleven-year-old without shame.

passage:
Every evening in their village near Hubli, Kavitha, ten, practised kabaddi in the dusty ground behind the school. Raid, touch, back. Raid, touch, back. Her knees were always scraped.
At the district festival, her team reached the final against Uday's team from the next village. They lost by two points.
Kavitha felt tears come. She wanted to kick the dust.
Instead she walked to Uday's team and shook hands. “Good game. Your ankle hold is really good.”
Uday grinned. “Your raids too.”
The next evening, Kavitha was back behind the school, practising the ankle hold.

qa.q: How many points did Kavitha's team lose by?
qa.a: They lost by two points.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel after losing the final?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and upset, with tears coming.

qa.q: What showed good sportsmanship in Kavitha?
qa.a: She shook hands, congratulated the winners and praised their skill.

qa.q: How might Uday feel when Kavitha praises his team?
qa.a: He probably feels respected and happy, praising her back.

grounding: A ten-year-old practises daily and loses a final gracefully.

passage:
At the tennis club in Buenos Aires, Hana, eleven, stayed after training every Tuesday to practise her serve. Fifty serves. Most went into the net at first.
By the club tournament, she was getting half of them in.
In the semi-final she played Valentina, who had been playing for four years. Hana lost six games to three.
She walked to the net, shook hands and said, “Your backhand is amazing.”
Valentina smiled. “Your serve is getting really good.”
Hana smiled back. On the bus home she already planned next Tuesday's fifty serves.

qa.q: How many serves did Hana practise every Tuesday?
qa.a: Fifty serves.

qa.q: How did Hana feel after losing to Valentina?
qa.a: She felt disappointed but proud of her progress and motivated to keep practising.

qa.q: What does Hana's practice routine show about skill building?
qa.a: It shows that repeated practice slowly makes a skill better.

qa.q: How did Valentina respond to Hana's handshake?
qa.a: She smiled and praised Hana's serve.

grounding: An eleven-year-old builds skill through practice and loses a match gracefully.

passage:
At the chess club in the community centre, Reena, twelve, had been practising openings every evening for three weeks. She had them written in a notebook.
In the final, she played Minakshi. For twenty minutes it was even. Then Reena made a mistake and lost her queen. She lost the game.
She stared at the board. Her throat tightened.
Then she held out her hand. “Well played. How did you see that move?”
Minakshi showed her. Reena wrote it in her notebook.
The club coach said, “That's how champions learn.”

qa.q: How long had Reena been practising openings?
qa.a: Every evening for three weeks.

qa.q: How did Reena feel after losing her queen and the game?
qa.a: She felt upset and disappointed, her throat tightening.

qa.q: What did Reena do after losing that shows good sportsmanship and learning?
qa.a: She shook hands, praised Minakshi and asked how she saw the move, then wrote it down.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Reena asks about her move?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and respected, happy to share.

grounding: A twelve-year-old practises, loses gracefully and learns from her opponent.

passage:
When I was ten, I ate a packet of chips before every football practice. Salty, crunchy, and gone in a minute.
I'm Ujjwal. By the second half I'd be tired and slow.
Coach Dolma noticed. She asked what I'd eaten. When I told her, she didn't laugh. “Try a banana and a roti with something in it next time. See if your legs feel different.”
So I tried it for a week. Banana and a roti roll with egg.
By Friday I was running as fast in the second half as the first. I still like chips. Now they're for weekends.

qa.q: What did Coach Dolma suggest Ujjwal try?
qa.a: A banana and a roti with something in it.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel by Friday?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt stronger and pleased, running as fast in the second half as the first.

qa.q: Why did changing the snack help Ujjwal?
qa.a: The banana and roti gave longer-lasting energy than chips.

qa.q: How might Coach Dolma feel seeing Ujjwal run faster?
qa.a: She would probably feel pleased that her advice helped.

grounding: A student learns that food choices affect energy for sport.

passage:
Canteen note. Jagdish Singh, school canteen manager.
For most of the term, Baljeet (eleven) bought two samosas and a cold drink every lunch. By sixth period, his class teacher said, he was yawning.
After the health talk last week, I noticed a change. Baljeet stood at the counter, looked at the samosas, then asked for the dal-rice and a banana. He said, “Ma'am said this keeps you going longer.”
On Friday he came back and said he hadn't felt sleepy in maths.
Next step: I've put the fruit near the front of the counter, where children see it first.

qa.q: What did Baljeet usually buy before?
qa.a: Two samosas and a cold drink.

qa.q: How did Baljeet seem to feel after changing his lunch?
qa.a: He seemed pleased and more awake, not sleepy in maths.

qa.q: Why is putting fruit near the front a good next step?
qa.a: It makes healthy choices easier for children to see and pick.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's class teacher feel about the change?
qa.a: The teacher is probably pleased to see him more awake in class.

grounding: A canteen manager notes an eleven-year-old linking food choices to energy.

passage:
Wednesday
Mumma gave me an apple for my tiffin. I wanted the packaged mango juice like my cousin Ujjwal has.
Ujjwal told me his coach said those juices have lots of added sugar and don't fill you up. I didn't believe him.
So today I tried an experiment. Monday: juice at break. I was hungry again by eleven. Today: the apple and some peanuts. I wasn't hungry till lunch.
Ujjwal said, “See?” I said, “Okay, okay.”
I'll still have juice sometimes. But not every day. — Dhruv

qa.q: What did Mumma give Dhruv for the tiffin?
qa.a: An apple.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel about Ujjwal's advice at first, and then?
qa.a: Dhruv felt doubtful at first, then convinced after the experiment.

qa.q: What did Dhruv's experiment show?
qa.a: The apple and peanuts kept Dhruv full longer than the juice.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel after Dhruv's experiment?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably feels pleased, and a bit smug, to be proved right.

grounding: A student tests how food choices affect energy and fullness.

passage:
“Ow! My knee!” Hafsa, nine, sat on the lane beside her fallen cycle, blood on her knee.
Binita, eleven, ran over. “Don't touch it with dirty hands. Can you move it?”
“Yes. It stings.”
“Stay here.” Binita ran to her house, came back with a bottle of clean water and a clean handkerchief. “This might sting.” She poured the water gently, then pressed the cloth on it.
“It's not stopping!”
“It's slowing. Keep pressing.” Binita took out her phone. “What's your Ammi's number?”
Hafsa told her. Binita called. “Aunty, Hafsa fell off her cycle. She's okay but her knee is cut. We're at the corner.”

qa.q: What did Binita bring back from her house?
qa.a: A bottle of clean water and a clean handkerchief.

qa.q: How was Hafsa feeling after she fell?
qa.a: She felt hurt and scared, saying it stung and wasn't stopping.

qa.q: What first-aid steps did Binita take, and why were they sensible?
qa.a: She kept dirty hands off, washed it with clean water, pressed a clean cloth, and called an adult.

qa.q: How might Hafsa's Ammi feel when she gets the call?
qa.a: She may feel worried but relieved that Binita stayed calm and called quickly.

grounding: An eleven-year-old handles a friend's small injury and calls a parent.

passage:
Last winter, when I was ten, Anirban-dadu slipped in the bathroom and couldn't get up. Everyone else was out.
I'm Kalyani. My hands were shaking. But I remembered what we practised at school: stay calm, don't try to lift someone heavy, call for help.
I put a pillow under his head. Then I called 112 on his phone. I said, “My grandfather has fallen and can't get up. Our address is Flat 3B, Lake View Apartments, Salt Lake.” I stayed with him and talked to him till the ambulance came.
The doctor said I did the right thing. I still remember my voice shaking.

qa.q: What number did Kalyani call?
How did Kalyani feel when Anirban-dadu fell?
qa.a: Kalyani felt frightened, with shaking hands, but stayed calm enough to help.

qa.q: What steps did Kalyani take, and why were they right?
qa.a: Kalyani didn't try to lift him, put a pillow under his head, called 112 with a clear address and stayed with him.

qa.q: How might Anirban-dadu have felt while waiting for the ambulance?
qa.a: He probably felt scared and in pain but comforted that Kalyani was with him.

grounding: A student remembers emergency steps and calls for help when a grandfather falls.

passage:
PE teacher's note. Jagdish Rao.
At Monday's assembly in the heat, a Class 5 boy fainted in the line.
Maria (twelve) acted quickly. She told the children near him to step back and give him air. She sent one friend running to the staffroom for me and another to the office to call the nurse. She stayed with him and kept talking to him until he opened his eyes.
When I arrived, she explained clearly what had happened and when.
The nurse took over and called his parents. He is fine.
Next step: Maria will help me teach the Class 5 emergency drill.

qa.q: What happened at Monday's assembly?
qa.a: A Class 5 boy fainted in the line.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when the boy fainted?
qa.a: She probably felt frightened but focused, staying calm enough to help.

qa.q: What did Maria do that made her response effective?
qa.a: She gave the boy space, sent friends to get adults and stayed with him, then explained clearly.

qa.q: How might the fainted boy feel when he opens his eyes and sees Maria?
qa.a: He may feel confused but reassured that someone was looking after him.

grounding: A PE teacher notes a twelve-year-old calling for help and managing a small emergency.

passage:
In the village school near Aizawl, Ms Lalremsiami drew a simple outline on the board.
“The parts covered by your swimsuit are private,” she said. “No one may touch them, or ask you to keep a secret about them. Not a stranger, not someone you know.”
Chandrika, ten, put up her hand. “What if we tell someone and they don't listen?”
“Then you tell someone else. And someone else. Until someone believes you.”
Each child wrote three trusted adults on a card. Chandrika wrote: Ma, Ms Lalremsiami, my Aunty Sanga.
She folded the card and kept it in her pencil box.

qa.q: How many trusted adults did each child write down?
qa.a: Three trusted adults.

passage:
After school in Lagos, Yara, nine, lingered by Mr Emeka's desk until the others left.
“Sir… Uncle Tunde next door made me sit on his lap and touched me where it's private. He said it's our secret.”
Mr Emeka stayed very calm and put down his pen. “Thank you for telling me, Yara. You were brave. It is not your fault.”
He didn't leave her alone. He asked a colleague to fetch the head of safeguarding, Mrs Adeyemi, while he sat with Yara. Mrs Adeyemi came at once, listened, and called Yara's mother that afternoon. Together they made a plan so Yara would not go next door again.

qa.q: Who did Mr Emeka ask a colleague to fetch?
qa.a: The head of safeguarding, Mrs Adeyemi.

qa.q: How was Yara feeling when she lingered by the desk?
qa.a: She felt scared and uneasy, carrying a secret she knew was wrong.

qa.q: What did Mr Emeka do that made him a safe adult?
qa.a: He stayed calm, thanked her, told her it was not her fault, stayed with her and got the safeguarding lead the same day.

qa.q: How might Yara's mother feel when Mrs Adeyemi calls?
qa.a: She would likely be shocked and upset, but grateful Yara told a trusted adult.

grounding: A nine-year-old tells her teacher about unsafe touch, and the school responds the same day.

passage:
At break, Omkar, eleven, found his friend Nikhil sitting alone on the stairs.
“What's wrong?”
Nikhil twisted his fingers. “The tuition sir plays a secret game. He touches me. He says don't tell or I'll fail.”
Omkar felt his stomach drop. “That's not okay. That's not a game.”
“Don't tell anyone!”
“We have to. It's not your fault. Come with me.”
Omkar walked Nikhil straight to Ms Uma, the counsellor. She listened calmly, told Nikhil he was brave and not to blame, and called his parents while both boys sat in her room. She said she would report it that same day.

qa.q: What did the tuition sir say would happen if Nikhil told?
qa.a: He said Nikhil would fail.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when Nikhil told him?
qa.a: He felt shocked and worried, his stomach dropping.

qa.q: Why was going to Ms Uma the right step?
qa.a: It got a trusted adult involved immediately who could protect Nikhil and report the abuse.

qa.q: How might Nikhil feel after Ms Uma responds?
qa.a: He may feel frightened but relieved and safer, knowing he is believed.

grounding: An eleven-year-old helps a friend tell a counsellor about abuse, and she acts the same day.

passage:
When I was eleven I got twenty rupees pocket money every week. I spent it on chips and cola with my friend Jasleen after school.
I'm Tanuja. Then I saw a cricket bat in the sports shop. It cost a lot more than I had.
I made a chart on my wall, with a box for each week. Every time I skipped the snacks, I coloured a box. Some weeks I gave in and bought chips. Jasleen teased me.
After four months, I had enough. I bought the bat myself.
When I hit my first six with it, I felt richer than any packet of chips.

qa.q: What did Tanuja see in the sports shop?
qa.a: A cricket bat.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel on hitting the first six with the new bat?
qa.a: Tanuja felt proud and happy, richer than any packet of chips.

qa.q: What helped Tanuja reach the goal?
qa.a: A chart to track each week, and choosing the bat over snacks most weeks.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel after seeing the bat?
qa.a: Jasleen may feel impressed, even after teasing Tanuja.

grounding: A student saves pocket money toward a goal, choosing it over impulse snacks.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 6 school fair activity. Sudha Iyer.
Each child had fifty paper rupees to spend at the class market. The task: buy a notebook, a pencil, and one fun thing.
Kiran (eleven) went straight to the toy stall and spent forty on a spinning top. Then he had only ten left, not enough for the notebook.
He looked upset. “I didn't think.”
We talked about needs and wants. He traded the top back for the notebook, pencil and a small eraser.
He said, “Next time I'll buy the needs first.”
Next step: I'll repeat the activity next term.

qa.q: How much did Kiran spend on the spinning top?
qa.a: He spent forty on a spinning top.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when he couldn't buy the notebook?
qa.a: He felt upset and frustrated with himself.

qa.q: What did Kiran learn from the activity?
qa.a: To buy needs first before spending on wants.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel when Kiran says he'll buy needs first?
qa.a: The teacher would likely feel pleased that he learned from his mistake.

grounding: A teacher records an eleven-year-old learning to prioritise needs over wants.

passage:
Monday
I'm saving for a football. I have half the money in my tin.
Today at the stationery shop there was a shiny keychain with a light in it. I really wanted it. Vishal said, “Just buy it. It's small.”
I held it for a long time. Then I thought, if I buy this, the football takes longer.
I put it back. Vishal said I was boring.
When I got home I counted my tin again. Still half. But half is closer than less than half.
I'm going to play football with the old ball tomorrow. — Harish

qa.q: What did Harish see at the stationery shop?
qa.a: A shiny keychain with a light in it.

qa.q: How did Harish feel while holding the keychain?
qa.a: Harish felt tempted and torn between the keychain and the football.

qa.q: What choice did Harish make, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: Harish put the keychain back to keep saving for the football, which was the bigger goal.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Harish's choice?
qa.a: Vishal thinks Harish is boring for not buying the keychain.

grounding: A student resists an impulse buy to keep saving toward a goal.
